title: Anna Ruadh takes An Taigh-òsta Grianach's charter to stone
summary: The keeper of An Taigh-òsta Grianach on the road to Cnoc leathan, who has mended the stretch out of her own household's stores for three generations, asks Anna Ruadh that the new charter be cut in stone rather than skin, since a fire can lose a skin but never a stone, and the queen has it cut before she leaves the district.

title: An old fisher of Ceann mhin judges the queen fair to the fish
summary: Years after Anna Ruadh's ruling that both fishers and carriers might carry the dried catch inland, an old fisher of the strand, asked which side the queen had truly favoured, answers that she had favoured the fish, which was more than either household carrying it had thought to do.

title: Fearchar Ruadh wins the stone field at Ceann leathan
summary: A mason's apprentice named Fearchar Ruadh of Doire mhin takes the silver ring at Anna Ruadh's new stone-walled contest field, and eats the crown's meal at the same board as every man he beat under the queen's own new law, a custom he is said never afterward to have forgotten at any table.

title: The wood-watcher reads a message home before it comes
summary: In Anna Ruadh's household at Cathair dhearg the wood-watcher out of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag reads the crossing of three geese and tells the queen, unasked, that a message she had given up waiting for will come within the week; an answer to a year-old letter reaches her on the sixth day, and no one in the household troubles him with idle questions after.

title: Cathair dhomhain doubles its own strictness in answer
summary: Cathair dhomhain's shrine, stung by the capital's wood-watcher, doubles its own cutter's visits to Coimheadaiche na Lasrach's measure without being asked, and for a hundred years after a Cathair dhomhain man swearing an oath is known on the roads by how exactly he keeps to its letter.

title: Anna Ruadh's second circuit
summary: Anna Ruadh walks the whole road circuit a second time in her middle years, slower than her first walking, stopping longest where keepers who fed her as a young queen feed her again grey-haired; at Am Buabhall Fortanach she sleeps a night under the same roof for the only time in either circuit.

title: Coinneach Bàn begins the copying of the provincial rolls
summary: Coinneach Bàn, choosing a clerk's work over his mother's roads, has every province seat send its own laws to Cathair dhearg to be copied fresh, and reads each copy through himself before it is shelved, so that within a decade a province's own clerks trust the capital's copy of their rolls sooner than the damp-spoiled skins in their own keeping.

title: A second clerk keeps the unstruck preface
summary: Before the knife reaches Clàr an Talla, the clerk Seumas Bàn sends for has already made a copy of the count of his own house for his own hand; it is that unstruck copy, kept quietly through the rest of the age, and not the scraped preface, that answers for the fact today.

title: Ealasaid Bhàn writes the hawk-keepers' refusal into hide
summary: Ealasaid Bhàn, eldest of the fowler households of Seann Skell, meets Talla na Lasrach's cutter Ruairidh Òg at her own door and tells him the dawn measure is the hawk's and not Coimheadaiche na Lasrach's, allowing him only to watch from the yard as any neighbour might, and setting the answer down in a strip of hide so that no cutter after him could mistake it.

title: A guard swears the wolf-sworn's graver oath at Caol leathan
summary: A young road-guard swears the first of the graver oaths at Caol leathan's new hall, hand flat on the white stone in a room still smelling of fresh mortar, and tells his own household after that the stone had felt warm under his palm, though the mason who set it swears he cut and laid nothing but plain grey rock from the town's own quarry.

title: A gravestone-cutter carves Seann Vell's scorpion from a fisherman's telling
summary: The stonecutter who carves Seann Vell's yellow scorpion, better known till then for gravestones than for shrines, works from a fisherman's account of one washed up dead on the strand, having no living creature shown to her, so that the image every child of the town learns to fear owes as much to a fisher's memory as to the god it serves.

title: The wood-watchers judge a boundary quarrel under the trees
summary: A cutter of Cnoc bhàn and a fowler of the Abhainn ìseal bring a boundary quarrel to the wood-watchers of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag rather than to Dùn ìseal, and both accept a judgement neither asked for: that the disputed scrub belongs to whoever feeds it through a hard winter, and to no one in an easy one.

title: The council's carpenters set the hawk-keepers nearest the door
summary: The carpenters who build the council's new benches at Dùn ìseal, told only the number of heads for each company, set the hawk-keepers' bench nearest the door for no reason any clerk troubles to record, so that latecomers of every company after sit longest among strangers before reaching their own.

title: Beathag Fhionn rules the springs open to every company
summary: Beathag Fhionn, keeper of the bath-house over Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh at Muileann ruadh, rules that the sick of every rite shall be carried up and bathed at dawn without being asked first which company they keep, and every province seat with a copy of anything at all copies her ruling into its own rolls that same season.
